rationale: Sohns et al. (2021) conduct a qualitative participatory modeling study using individual interviews and follow-up questionnaires with 14 water policy stakeholders in Alaska to construct individual and merged causal loop diagrams (CLDs) of rural household water vulnerability. Across the economic, infrastructure, and social sub-models and policy themes, multiple governance and legal mechanisms are co-equally examined: intergovernmental fiscal allocation and decentralization (federal/state capital vs. O&M funding splits, state revenue sharing, 1% State Revolving Fund share, and multi-level coordination across decentralized villages; institutional_structure_coordination, the most pervasive structural driver), tariff structures and subsidies (flat monthly vs. volumetric watering-point charges, high-burden rates, and user-fee/O&M subsidies; fees_tariffs_subsidies), stringent water quality and O&M regulatory standards (enforcement_sanctions), competitive grant-writing, operator exam, and permitting barriers (procedural_burden), and utility ownership/regionalized collaborative models (regulatory_model_ownership). The focal problem variable, household water vulnerability, primarily captures effective_access (water quantity, safe quality, fewer non-functional system days, and hauling distance), alongside central co-modeled dimensions of economic_access (household water affordability) and primary_connection (construction of in-home piped water systems versus unserved/haul communities).
